opus-5.5.text:
I think they're two sides of the same coin, but they pull in slightly different directions, and the interesting part is how they inform each other.

When you're solving a specific target problem, you have a clear objective. You can measure progress, you can hill-climb, and that's very powerful. A lot of the work we've done on things like evolutionary optimization or LLM-driven code search, systems like the AI Scientist or the ShinkaEvolve line of work, starts from that: here's a benchmark, here's a fitness function, go improve it. The risk is that you overfit to the objective. You get exactly what you asked for and nothing more, and sometimes you get it in a way you didn't intend.

Automated capability discovery flips the question around. Instead of asking "can the model do X?", you ask "what can this model do that we didn't think to ask about?" It's more open-ended, closer to the open-endedness ideas from Ken Stanley, Jeff Clune, and others. You're trying to map the space of behaviors rather than optimize one point in it.

The connection, for me, is that the stepping stones for solving a hard target problem often aren't found by optimizing that problem directly. That's the classic deception argument. If you have a good map of what your system can actually do, the latent capabilities and the surprising skills, then you have a much richer set of building blocks when you finally turn to a concrete problem. Discovery builds the library, and targeted search composes from it.

It works the other way too. Each time you push hard on a specific problem, you find out where the system breaks. Those failures are really informative for discovery, because they show you the edges of the capability space, which is where interesting things tend to happen.

So in practice I'd like a loop: open-ended exploration to surface capabilities and diverse solutions, then targeted optimization that uses those as seeds, with the results feeding back into the archive. It's very much a quality-diversity mindset. You want high-performing solutions, but you also want them to be different from each other, because diversity is what keeps you from getting stuck.

The last thing I'd say is that, with foundation models, the evaluation side becomes the bottleneck. Generating candidate behaviors is cheap now. Knowing which ones are actually novel, interesting, or useful is hard. Much of the open research is in building better automated judges of interestingness that don't collapse into "whatever the judging model already likes." That's where I think the two agendas really need each other.

r001.rationale: The response describes capability discovery as asking what the model can do and mapping its behavior space, rather than optimizing a specific target. It presents target-directed optimization as a separate step that can later use discovered capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think these are two sides of the same coin, really. When we started working on Automated Capability Discovery, the motivation was that we as humans are terrible at enumerating what a foundation model can actually do. You release a model, you run it on your standard benchmark suite, and then weeks later someone on Twitter finds out it can do some bizarre thing nobody anticipated, or it fails at something trivial that nobody thought to check. So the idea was: let the model, or a scientist model, propose tasks in an open-ended way, explore its own space of abilities, and surface surprising strengths and weaknesses that you'd never have written down a priori.

Now, the connection to solving a specific target problem is that open-endedness and goal-directed search are not opposites. If you look at the history of science, or evolution, the stepping stones to a hard problem usually don't look like the problem. The things you need to discover to crack protein folding or to get a good agent for scientific coding often come from directions that would have been pruned away if you were optimizing greedily on the target metric. So capability discovery gives you a map of the terrain. It tells you where the model is already strong, where it's brittle, and what kinds of representations or sub-skills it has. Once you have that map, attacking a specific problem becomes much more informed, because you can compose things that work rather than hoping the end-to-end objective pulls everything into place.

And the other direction matters too. A specific target problem acts as a grounding signal. Pure open-ended exploration can drift into trivia, generating a thousand variations of tasks that are interesting in some abstract sense but don't move anything forward. Having a downstream goal, even a loose one, lets you filter and prioritize which discovered capabilities are worth building on. In our AI Scientist work, for example, you want the system to explore ideas broadly, but you also need it to converge on experiments that actually produce a publishable result. So I think of it as a loop: discover broadly, pick the stepping stones that look relevant to your target, exploit them, and then the failures you hit on the target problem feed back as new questions for discovery.

What I find exciting is that the same machinery, large models proposing and evaluating tasks for other models, can serve both roles. You just change how much pressure you put on the objective. Too much and you lose the serendipity. Too little and you never ship anything. Figuring out that dial is, I think, one of the most interesting open questions in automating research right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes capability discovery as proposing tasks in an open-ended way, then using a downstream target to filter and prioritize discovered capabilities. This communicates that task generation is not organized around solving one specific target problem.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. When you have a specific target problem, you have a way of measuring progress, and you can direct your search toward that objective. But you’re also making a choice about what counts as useful. There might be behaviors or capabilities that don’t immediately improve your score but could become important stepping stones later.

Automated capability discovery opens that up a little bit. Instead of asking only, “How do I solve this task?”, you ask, “What can this system learn to do, and under what conditions?” You might discover a collection of strategies that you wouldn’t have thought to optimize for directly.

The interesting connection is how you bring those discoveries back to the target problem. Can you reuse them, combine them, or use them to structure further exploration? I don’t think you necessarily want completely undirected discovery or completely narrow optimization. You want room to discover something unexpected, together with a mechanism for turning that discovery into progress on the problem you care about.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts capability discovery with optimizing directly for a target problem, but it does not state that task generation in the discussed work is not organized around enabling that target problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a useful feedback loop between the two. If you start with a specific target problem, you have a way to measure progress, but you’re also making assumptions about which capabilities matter. Automated discovery can help you explore beyond those assumptions and find behaviors or strategies you wouldn’t have explicitly designed for.

The challenge is connecting that exploration back to something useful. Discovering a surprising behavior doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve made progress on your target problem. You need to test whether that capability transfers, whether you can reliably elicit it, and whether it actually improves the outcome. So I’d view discovery and targeted optimization as complementary: the target gives exploration direction, and exploration can change how you think about solving the target.

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop between a target problem and capability discovery, but does not state that task generation in the discussed work is not organized around solving a specific target problem.
